query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Wear performance in high‐entropy alloy protective coatings is governed by their ability to form and maintain an ultra‐nanocrystalline (or dynamically refined) near‐surface layer during sliding contact, which reduces friction and wear by limiting stress localization at the contact interface.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy coating with a conventional, relatively coarse or mixed grain structure (e.g., as found in CoCrFeMnNi or AlCoCrFeNi systems prepared by standard methods)
generation.intervention: Engineer a controlled microstructural change prior to wear testing by refining the coating’s grain size (e.g., via processing modifications or controlled alloying additions) so that it starts with a nanocrystalline structure that is predisposed to form a protective surface layer under sliding.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding wear tests conducted at room temperature and moderate elevated temperatures under inert or controlled environments, ensuring that oxidation effects are minimized.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and stabilization of an ultra‐nanocrystalline, or dynamically refined, surface layer (i.e., a nano‐glaze) that evolves during wear.
generation.mechanism: Under the applied shear of sliding wear, mechanical energy triggers grain refinement and possible amorphization near the surface. This adaptive nanocrystalline layer distributes the contact stress, enhances hardness locally, and reduces adhesive and abrasive wear mechanisms by lowering the interfacial friction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings with an artificially pre-refined (nanocrystalline) microstructure will exhibit lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates compared to baseline coatings with a coarser initial grain structure because the protective layer forms more rapidly and remains more stable during sliding.
generation.baseline: Coatings produced by standard processing that have larger or mixed grain sizes, where the protective ultra-nanocrystalline layer forms only as a wear-induced transformation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in high-entropy alloy coatings with similar compositional complexity (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi, AlCoCrFeNi) under wear conditions where oxidation is minimal. In highly oxidative or extremely high-temperature environments, other mechanisms (such as reactive oxide formation) may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The critical initial grain-size threshold and exact compositional dependencies required to reliably trigger and sustain the adaptive ultra-nanocrystalline layer remain to be quantitatively determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy coatings: one with the conventional (coarser) microstructure and one with an engineered pre-refined nanocrystalline structure achieved by modifying processing parameters. Subject both sets to identical dry sliding wear tests under controlled laboratory conditions.
measurements: Wear rate (mm³/N-m) using standardized wear testing
Hardness profiles near the worn surface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings with the pre-refined nanocrystalline structure do not show a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear rate compared to the baseline coatings, or if both types develop similar protective surface layers regardless of initial grain size, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Synthesis and Mechanical Characterization of a CuMoTaWV High-Entropy Film by Magnetron Sputtering

Abstract: Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2).
